newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italy sees ERM return soon but Prodi cautious.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italy sees ERM return soon but Prodi cautious.

text.p: Italy is resolved to return the vagabond lira to Europe's exchange rate mechanism after four years out in the cold but Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Friday tempered talk over timing of the politically charged event.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi and Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco both indicated in the past week that Italy will apply to return to the currency grid later in November and even hinted at what exchange parities against the mark might be.
But Prodi, on a trip to Austria on Friday, said there was no set date for the lira's re-entry into the ERM, although Italy was likely to apply to return this year.
"There is no precise date. In due time we shall start the process of application for re-entry in the ERM," he said.
Meanwhile market watchers are assessing at what rate against the mark the lira can be reinstated and politicians, industrialists and economists are pitching into the debate.

Visco was the latest to join the chorus, telling a meeting late on Thursday: "I think a balanced solution with the mark between 1,000 and 1,050 lire would be more than reasonable, especially as we are in a situation in which we still have a little potential competitive advantage."
Ciampi, a former prime minister and central bank governor, earlier cited a possible rate "slightly above 1,000 per mark".

Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, another ex-prime minister and central banker, said it would be hard for anyone to impose a rate out of line with the level the lira has held for months on foreign exchange markets.
But Italian industry wants a weaker level of 1,050, with Giorgio Fossa, chairman of employers' association Confindustria, saying this was compatible with Italy's high interest rates.

The lira's parity within the ERM is a bone of contention with Italy's EU partners. French industrialists complain they have been hit by the competitive edge enjoyed by Italian producers as a result of heavy depreciation.

In Brussels, European Union officials said the central parity was such a sensitive issue that EU finance ministers may have decide the rate instead of the customary monetary committee of finance ministry and central bank officials.

Shortly before it left the ERM in September 1992 the lira had a central rate of 802.49 per mark and 239.27 per French franc but by early 1995 it had plummeted to a historic low of 1,275 per mark, a depreciation of more than 50 percent, and to 359.80 per franc. It is now around 298.00 against the franc.

Since 1995 the lira has risen with Italy's political fortunes, holding at 990 to 1,010 per mark since September. Foreign exchange dealers suspect the steadying hand of the Bank of Italy has intervened to prevent further appreciation.

Economists say based on the performance of the lira in the past six months, a rate of 1,010-1,020 would be reasonable. Marcello Pericoli, economist at San Paolo bank in London, saw Italy asking for 1,025, slightly weaker than today's level as Italian interest rates were expected to fall by the year end.
But several analysts point out that, given the political stakes, a level of around 1,000 may be more likely.
Stephen King, chief European economist at HSBC Markets, said a trade-off was needed between Italy's ideal of 1,050 and France's preference for something closer to 950.

"A thousand would seem to be a reasonable compromise and given we've been trading at approximately 1,000 for the last three or four months it does look as though that's the kind of implicit target the Italians are aiming for," King said.
